scenarios.title: A worker is killed in the middle of a job
scenarios.broke: Started a real worker process on a 4-second job and killed it with SIGKILL one second in: no shutdown, no cleanup, no chance to say anything.
scenarios.expected: The job is not lost and not run twice: its lease runs out, a second worker claims it, and it finishes exactly once.
scenarios.observed: A second worker finished it 7.2 s after the kill (the 3-second lease running out, plus starting the new worker and redoing the 4-second job), on attempt 2. The killed worker's half-done work never committed.

scenarios.title: The event relay crashes after sending, before recording it
scenarios.broke: Made the relay publish an event and then fail before it could mark the event as sent, the worst moment for a message system to die.
scenarios.expected: The event is sent again on the next pass (at least once), and the consumer ignores the repeat (applied exactly once).
scenarios.observed: The event was delivered on 2 passes and applied 1 time. The repeat was recognised by its id and skipped.

scenarios.title: Eight workers fight over the same queue
scenarios.broke: Put 200 jobs on the queue and let 8 workers grab them as fast as they could, all at once.
scenarios.expected: Every job is handed to exactly one worker: none skipped, none done twice.
scenarios.observed: 200 of 200 jobs claimed, 0 handed out twice, at about 2,161 jobs a second.

scenarios.title: The same upload arrives 20 times at once
scenarios.broke: Fired 20 simultaneous requests to queue processing for the same recording, as a flaky network retrying would.
scenarios.expected: One job is queued; the other 19 are recognised as repeats.

scenarios.title: A job that crashes every time
scenarios.broke: Queued a job whose code always throws an error, next to an ordinary job.
scenarios.expected: The bad job is retried after a pause, then parked for a person to look at. It never blocks the queue.
scenarios.observed: The healthy job finished on the first pass, 55 ms in. The bad one failed 2 times, 5 s apart, and was parked as dead with its error kept.

scenarios.title: The AI provider goes down
scenarios.broke: Made the AI provider fail every call, then sent 20 more requests while it was down, then brought it back.
scenarios.expected: After a few failures the system stops calling the broken provider, refuses instantly instead of hanging, and tries again on its own after a cool-down.
scenarios.observed: The circuit opened after 3 failed calls. All 20 follow-up calls were refused in at most 0.006 ms without touching the provider. One second later a trial call went through and the circuit closed.

scenarios.title: The database disappears
scenarios.broke: Started a real server pointed at a database that does not exist.
scenarios.expected: The server stays alive and says what is wrong, but tells the load balancer to stop sending it traffic. Pages that need no data still load.
scenarios.observed: /health answered 200 (degraded), /ready answered 503 so a load balancer routes away, and the public pages still served 200. Both checks answered in 26 ms instead of hanging.

scenarios.title: The shared cache (Redis) goes away
scenarios.broke: Started a real server configured to use a Redis server that is not there.
scenarios.expected: A cache outage makes the system slower, never broken: every request still succeeds, and the health check reports the cache as down.
scenarios.observed: All 3 pages answered 200. /health reported the cache as down (redis), so an operator sees it while users don't.

scenarios.title: One visitor floods the site
scenarios.broke: Sent 300 requests for the same page from one address, all at once.
scenarios.expected: The first 120 in the minute are served, the rest get a polite 'slow down' with a time to retry, and the server keeps answering everyone else.
scenarios.observed: 120 served, 180 told to slow down (every one with a Retry-After time), in 0.9 s. The health check right after answered in 15 ms.
